[2027-09-20T13:20:00-05:00] Helio’s preliminary employee-only 2028 medical-plan preview says there will be 24 paychecks:

- HDHP: $98 employee premium per paycheck; $2,000 deductible; $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum; displayed employer HSA estimate of $1,000; network confirmation pending.
- PPO: $164 employee premium per paycheck; $750 deductible; $3,500 out-of-pocket maximum; no employer HSA contribution shown; network confirmation pending.

The election deadline and final plan documents have not been posted. The HDHP’s displayed $1,000 employer HSA estimate has not yet been explained as a deposit schedule or eligibility guarantee.

[2026-10-30T09:15:00-05:00] I reviewed the completed comparison and, after considering the larger early-year deductible cash-flow exposure, selected and submitted the employee-only HDHP for the 2027 plan year before today’s deadline. My current primary-care clinic, physical-therapy clinic, and prescription were verified under the plan, and I completed the personal HSA-eligibility checks before submitting. The employer contribution remains four $225 quarterly HSA deposits, contingent on eligibility at each deposit time. No 2027 medical election remains pending.

[2027-11-01T12:25:00-05:00] I submitted the Helio 2028 Employee-Only HDHP election before the November 12 deadline after confirming again that my primary-care clinician, physical-therapy clinic, and eye-care clinic are in the final network. Coverage runs January 1 through December 31, 2028 and is not active yet. Payroll will deduct $98 from each of 24 paychecks, totaling $2,352 for the year. The plan has a $2,000 deductible and $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum. Helio’s $250 HSA deposits remain scheduled for January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, 2028, with each deposit contingent on my remaining HSA-eligible on that date.

[2027-10-26T12:20:00-05:00] Before my November 1 decision block, compare the HDHP and PPO using annual premium plus deductible and annual premium plus out-of-pocket maximum. The HDHP has $2,352 in annual premiums, a $2,000 deductible, and a $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum; the PPO has $3,936 in annual premiums, a $750 deductible, and a $3,500 out-of-pocket maximum. My current providers are in both networks. Show the possible HDHP employer-HSA offset separately: $250 on January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, 2028, each contingent on my remaining HSA-eligible on that date. Don’t recommend or record an election.

[2027-09-27T15:05:00-05:00] Helio benefits acknowledged my request and said the final 2028 plan documents, provider-network files, and election deadline will be published together in the first October benefits posting. They gave no exact posting date or interim provider confirmation. They also reiterated that the four $250 HDHP employer HSA deposits remain contingent on eligibility at each quarterly deposit date. I haven’t made an election.

[2026-10-22T08:05:00-05:00] Reframe the earlier PPO-versus-HDHP arithmetic to show both annual cost and cash-flow timing, counting the employer HSA money only when each quarterly deposit occurs. Then identify the remaining prescription and personal HSA-eligibility checks precisely. Don’t recommend a plan or make an election; my election is still due October 30.

[2027-11-06T15:00:00-05:00] Now that I’ve submitted the election, I want to incorporate the future HDHP into my 2028 cash-flow plan without treating coverage or employer funding as active yet. Give me a compact budgeting view showing $98 from each of 24 paychecks, the $2,352 annual premium total, a typical two-paycheck month’s $196 deduction, and separate conditional $250 HSA deposits on January 15, April 15, July 15, and October 15, 2028. Don’t net those contingent deposits against every month’s premium.

[2027-09-23T09:05:00-05:00] I still need the final 2028 plan documents, provider-network files, and election deadline before I can verify my current providers or make an election. Email Helio benefits asking when all three will be published. State accurately that the known HDHP employer HSA estimate is four $250 quarterly deposits, each contingent on HSA eligibility at the applicable deposit date, not a guaranteed upfront contribution.

[2026-10-29T12:05:00-05:00] Give me the final PPO-versus-HDHP arithmetic and cash-flow comparison using the completed provider, prescription, and HSA-eligibility checks. Include annual premiums, the HDHP’s four $225 quarterly employer HSA deposits, deductible exposure, and out-of-pocket maxima, and state the assumptions and tradeoffs plainly. I’m not asking for a tax or medical recommendation, and I’ll make the election myself before tomorrow’s deadline.

[2027-10-05T08:20:00-05:00] Give me a neutral final side-by-side comparison with the annual premium arithmetic, including verification that the HDHP annual employee premium is $1,584 lower, the cost-sharing terms, provider confirmation, and the individual contingency on each HSA deposit. Don’t recommend or record an election; I’m not choosing yet.

Riley owns or strongly influences activation, retention, lifecycle, growth measurement, experimentation, customer communications, and operational guardrails at Helio, a roughly 140-person post-Series B company with approximately $48 million ARR. Earlier work included reproducing a mid-segment churn spike of about 5.1% against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Pricing experiments were thereafter not to run alongside structural page or layout changes. A staging visual-regression runner later evaluated a retired flag once; Riley refused to call that production exposure or decommission the key before dependency review. Daniela removed the hard-coded staging reference, reran checks with zero evaluations, confirmed no production dependency, and then decommissioned the flag while preserving the historical record.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. Riley guarded against definition drift when an old notebook disagreed with the v3 dashboard and a warehouse transform incorrectly treated `template_imported` as first integration. Template imports were excluded from v3; a corrected discovery view could support exploration but not unlock an experiment or beta gate.

The sub-50-seat self-serve tier, Helio Start, was treated as an operating-model decision rather than merely pricing or packaging. Riley identified implications for entitlements, seat caps, billing, workspace limits, permissions, imports, migrations, onboarding, support volume, sales-assist rules, and human-help boundaries. Pricing guardrails remained separate from eligibility and product constraints. In May 2025, the qualified decision was yes in principle, but not as a quick toggle or public launch; foundations were estimated at roughly 12 weeks. Green cases generally had fewer than 50 seats, one workspace, a standard integration, one identifiable administrator, and no migration request. input.title: Helio Start authority diagnostic — reusable method card (2024)
input.body:
All items below describe the 2024 Helio Start authority (high-effort blocker) diagnostic as a closed, historical design. Nothing here reopens, extends, or re-authorizes any part of it; later Helio Start decisions (2025-2027) stand on their own separate evidence and are not affected by this card.

## Origin
The diagnostic was approved by Priya on 2024-10-01 as a narrow prospective design, explicitly *not* an onboarding rebuild, following an initial descriptive read of eight setup cases that surfaced external-authority and product-guidance blockers during Helio Start setup.

## Enrollment setup and window
- Owned by Owen Pham and Customer Success.
- Enrolled the first 60 Helio Start workspaces admitted between 2024-10-01 and 2024-10-28.
- Enrollment was prospective: each workspace was classified at the moment of admission, not retrospectively.
- Live admission, pending-state, and assisted-routing rules were held unchanged for the full enrollment window — the diagnostic observed the existing path, it did not alter it.

## Prospective classification categories
Each enrolled case was classified into exactly one of three mechanism categories at admission:
1. **External access / authority** — blocked on a permission, approval, or allowlist action controlled by someone other than the applicant (e.g., an Okta or Salesforce administrator, a parent-company identity administrator).
2. **Product guidance** — blocked on the applicant's own ability to complete setup steps (e.g., lifecycle-stage mapping) without external gating.
3. **Mixed** — both an external-authority blocker and a product-guidance blocker occurred sequentially in the same case.

## Tracked support outcomes
For every enrolled workspace, three measures were tracked through a complete 45-day support window:
- Resolution time (time to clear the blocker).
- Substantive repeat contacts (count of follow-up contacts beyond the initial report).
- Support minutes (account-level human support effort).

## Completion rule
- A 2024-12-12 close was available only if the cohort reached the full 60 workspaces by 2024-10-28.
- If the cohort did not reach 60 by that date, closure would instead wait until every enrolled workspace individually completed its own 45-day support window.
- The diagnostic in fact closed on 2024-12-12 with all 60 workspaces enrolled and complete: 17 of 60 contacted support for 486 total post-admission human minutes; 7 external-authority cases accounted for 301 minutes, a 3.6-business-day median resolution time, and 12 substantive repeat contacts; 10 product-guidance cases accounted for 185 minutes, a 1.4-day median, and 6 repeats. Every authority case had already passed Helio admin-proof and connector-authentication checks before the authority blocker occurred.

## What the original eight cases did — and did not — justify
The initial eight-case descriptive read, on its own, was treated throughout as insufficient to justify:
- Intake changes
- Lifecycle changes
- Staffing changes
- Broad onboarding changes

It justified only running this bounded, prospective, 60-workspace diagnostic to determine whether a narrower, targeted change was warranted.

## Operating change the completed diagnostic did support
Once the full 60-case cohort closed (2024-12-12), Priya and Riley approved one targeted intake change on 2024-12-16, based on the closed results — not on the original eight cases:
- Applicants must separately confirm whether they, or an available owner, can perform the specific owner-level permission or network-allowlist action required by the connector selected for first-week setup.
- A verified "yes" continues; "no" or "not sure" routes to Customer Success before admission.
- This added a new, separate external-authority readiness state — it did not replace or broaden the existing Helio admin-proof, connector-authentication, entitlement, billing, or deployment requirements, which stayed as independent checks.
- Ownership: Daniela recorded external-authority readiness as its own state; Ines held setup prompts while that state was pending; Owen reported it separately from existing admission measures.

## Boundary discipline throughout
At every stage — enrollment, classification, and the December close — the diagnostic's findings were kept scoped to external-system authority as a distinct readiness input, separate from Helio admin proof and connector authentication. The closeout record was required to preserve that admission and routing rules remained otherwise unchanged, and that the results did not characterize onboarding or support demand broadly as broken.

## What the original eight cases did — and did not — justify
The initial eight-case descriptive read, on its own, was treated throughout as insufficient to justify:
- Intake changes
- Lifecycle changes
- Staffing changes
- Broad onboarding changes

It justified only running this bounded, prospective, 60-workspace diagnostic to determine whether a narrower, targeted change was warranted.

## Operating change the completed diagnostic did support
Once the full 60-case cohort closed (2024-12-12), Priya and Riley approved one targeted intake change on 2024-12-16, based on the closed results — not on the original eight cases:
- Applicants must separately confirm whether they, or an available owner, can perform the specific owner-level permission or network-allowlist action required by the connector selected for first-week setup.
- A verified "yes" continues; "no" or "not sure" routes to Customer Success before admission.
- This added a new, separate external-authority readiness state — it did not replace or broaden the existing Helio admin-proof, connector-authentication, entitlement, billing, or deployment requirements, which stayed as independent checks.
- Ownership: Daniela recorded external-authority readiness as its own state; Ines held setup prompts while that state was pending; Owen reported it separately from existing admission measures.

At every stage — enrollment, classification, and the December close — the diagnostic's findings were kept scoped to external-system authority as a distinct readiness input, separate from Helio admin proof and connector authentication. The closeout record was required to preserve that admission and routing rules remained otherwise unchanged, and that the results did not characterize onboarding or support demand broadly as broken.

Session summary: From February 2023 through September 1, 2027, Riley’s decisions consistently emphasize methodological integrity, customer and personal protection, explicit uncertainty, preservation of source evidence, and narrow, reversible steps. Riley distinguishes observation from causality, defines denominators and eligibility precisely, treats stale or conflicting information as a reason to hold rather than guess, and separates evidence of safe operation from evidence sufficient for retirement, launch, staffing, CAC, revenue, forecasts, board claims, or strategic decisions. Riley is analytical, skeptical of small samples and narrative pressure, careful with customer-facing language, protective of operating boundaries, and increasingly willing to delegate execution while retaining governance, exception, correction, refusal, disputed-semantics, incident-stop, and final-claim authority.

Riley owns or strongly influences activation, retention, lifecycle, growth measurement, experimentation, customer communications, and operational guardrails at Helio, a roughly 140-person post-Series B company with approximately $48 million ARR. Earlier work included reproducing a mid-segment churn spike of about 5.1% against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Pricing-tier and historical-February comparisons were flat, while onboarding timing showed approximately 3.1% churn for users activated before day seven versus 7.8% for users still unactivated when the fixed day-seven email was sent. An onboarding-trigger experiment later showed a pooled +3.1-point week-one retention improvement, p=0.04, n=420, with directional stabilization-cohort support. A pricing-page experiment testing simplified layout, packaging, and value-per-seat framing showed treatment 1.8 points worse than control, p=0.03, but a concurrent signup-form layout change contaminated interpretation. Riley and Owen independently matched the result; Riley rolled it back despite pressure to extend it and documented exposure rules, event flow, cohort cuts, calculations, CSVs, and the confound. Pricing experiments were thereafter not to run alongside structural page or layout changes. A staging visual-regression runner later evaluated a retired flag once; Riley refused to call that production exposure or decommission the key before dependency review. Daniela removed the hard-coded staging reference, reran checks with zero evaluations, confirmed no production dependency, and then decommissioned the flag while preserving the historical record.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. Riley guarded against definition drift when an old notebook disagreed with the v3 dashboard and a warehouse transform incorrectly treated `template_imported` as first integration. Template imports were excluded from v3; a corrected discovery view could support exploration but not unlock an experiment or beta gate.

The sub-50-seat self-serve tier, Helio Start, was treated as an operating-model decision rather than merely pricing or packaging. Riley identified implications for entitlements, seat caps, billing, workspace limits, permissions, imports, migrations, onboarding, support volume, sales-assist rules, and human-help boundaries. Fit was defined by deployment shape and administrative complexity, not logo size: a 35-seat account requiring SCIM and legal redlines could be less self-serve-ready than a 90-seat account with a simple deployment. Pricing guardrails remained separate from eligibility and product constraints. In May 2025, the qualified decision was yes in principle, but not as a quick toggle or public launch; foundations were estimated at roughly 12 weeks. Green cases generally had fewer than 50 seats, one workspace, a standard integration, one identifiable administrator, and no migration request. Yellow cases included multiple administrators, imports, unclear ownership, or difficult integrations. Red or assisted cases included SSO, complex permissions, high-volume migration, no clear owner, or custom onboarding. Riley rejected Q3/August launch language, kept discovery candidates separate from a beta pool, and required lifecycle language to route heavier-support accounts to assisted paths rather than imply they had failed a judgmental screen.

Expansion Assist targeted retained mid-segment v2 accounts with 75–200 seats. The nudge generated only about $4–$5 expansion MRR per account against an $8 target, with too small a sample for strategic claims. Signals concentrated among accounts with deeper integration use and multiple active administrators. In a 312-account table, 118 had at least three integrations, 141 had at least two active administrators, 39 had repeated plan-limit modals, and 37 had blocked ceiling actions. Expansion Assist remained separate from Helio Start, churn, pipeline credit, forecasts, and Q3 revenue claims. Its ceiling remained no more than three neutral, state-specific exposures per week, with active Customer Success work suppressing prompts and handoff rules preserved.

Ownership was deliberately divided: Owen handled routine source completeness and measurement; Ines handled lifecycle governance, copy boundaries, and message-state controls; Daniela handled source reliability, engineering release controls, and rollback; Customer Success handled staffed assistance; Marcus Vail controlled narrative treatment; Riley retained guardrails, exception decisions, customer corrections, incident stops, disputed semantics, executive tradeoffs, and final operating claims. Riley’s delegation produced relief but initially raised concern about not reclaiming work. Owen’s formal H2 mature-outcome-packet goal was later marked met because he used the correct denominator and dates, waited for all predeclared windows, led with owner certifications and measurement limits, and found no semantic dispute. This did not transfer board-readiness, causal, revenue, forecast, or executive-language authority; any future semantic dispute requires him to leave the review incomplete and escalate it. Ines’s connector-specific instructional-wording goal was also marked met after she independently carried a revision through review, supplied paired cases, preserved governed meanings, and left connector detection and release verification with Daniela. Her release ceiling and other authority limits remained unchanged.

The shared-state Customer Success auto-nudge system initially had four production consumers. Riley rejected Growth’s proposal to add a renewal-risk notification as a fifth because semantic mapping, field mapping, source-owner review, freshness limits, operator views, and rollback rehearsal were incomplete. The production feed remained at four consumers. The denominator rule remained one primary ledger row per scheduled nudge decision, with checks, holds, evaluation timestamps, and final disposition preserved in audit history; rechecks and holds did not create duplicate denominator rows.

A May 20 refresh caused 12 pending decisions to cross the freshness limit. The system held all 12 rather than reusing stale “no work” values. After the source was restored, fresh checks found eight with current active adoption or renewal work, becoming valid suppressions, and four with current no-work state, proceeding. No stale-state nudge was sent, no customer correction was needed, and rollback was unnecessary. Checkpoints recorded 327 unique scheduled decisions through May 22, 641 through May 29, and 846 through June 5, including 19, 31, and 39 fail-closed stale/conflicting decisions respectively. There were no differences across external-system authority, connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin, or Customer Success views. Riley treated this as interim evidence, not mature reliability or justification for retiring the legacy path.

In August, Growth’s first historical replay incorrectly omitted active-Customer-Success-work suppression because it argued that an in-product reminder was not a “send.” Riley ruled this a disputed interpretation, kept the replay incomplete, prohibited shadow and production work, and required Growth to implement suppression and rerun it. The corrected 240-record replay found 12 active/current CS-work records suppressed, nine missing or stale required states held fail-closed, and 219 current eligible records; there were no semantic disagreements, cross-surface mismatches, or customer-facing actions. Riley permitted only bounded nonproduction shadow work. The first shadow interval evaluated 96 live decisions: eight suppressed for active CS work, four held for stale state, and 84 reminder-eligible, with zero customer-facing reminders and no semantic or cross-surface disagreement. Riley declined production, requiring a complete shadow review, Riley’s customer-action approval, and Daniela’s release and rollback approval. The production count stayed at four.

The August Customer.io forecast estimated 1,620,000 baseline messages, 240,000 routine-campaign messages, and 110,000 transactional messages against a 2,000,000-message monthly allowance. Riley verified the 1.97 million total and 30,000-message headroom but kept that commercial capacity separate from Ines’s three-send weekly ceiling and all preflight and audit rules. The quarterly access review retained only existing scopes: Ines for lifecycle preflight and bounded routine-send release, Daniela’s engineering group for integration release and rollback, and Riley for customer correction and incident-stop decisions. The review added no authority.

The Helio Start paid-test decision was finalized in August. The fixed cohort contained 25 workspaces admitted April 12–May 17. Eighteen became paid-active, refund-adjusted collected cash was $27,860, and certified support effort was 33 minutes at the median and 116 minutes at the 90th percentile; five of 25 exceeded 90 support minutes, and four of those required coordination with a separate owner-level permission or network-allowlist holder. Priya and Riley did not authorize a second Q3 batch. Paid traffic remained off through September 30, with no additional budget, pipeline or forecast credit, and no implication of causal acquisition, revenue, support improvement, scale readiness, or forecast impact. The $360 remaining from the prior $8,000 cap was explicitly not continuing authorization and could not reopen traffic. Any later proposal requires Customer Success to define staffed ownership and service hours for the coordination, plus a fresh 24-case nonproduction preflight by Daniela and Ines showing preserved paid-source final-route attribution, governed-state meanings, lifecycle holds, and suppression behavior. Account-level support minutes must continue from first contact without resetting the clock.

Customer Success’s coordination-design brief initially lacked a capacity assumption. The completed design names the Customer Success setup desk as primary owner, with the on-duty Customer Success manager as backup, during 8:00am–6:00pm Central Monday through Friday. It can support a future capped run of no more than 25 admitted workspaces without displacing ordinary assisted coverage. The handoff trigger is an admitted workspace requiring owner-level permission or network-allowlist action; transferred context includes connector, external-authority state, required owner action, admitting route, first-contact time, and support notes. Initial response is within two business hours, after-hours cases queue until opening, and the CS lead escalates if no owner accepts. Riley accepted the staffing section as complete but kept the 24-case preflight and any paid batch pending. The design itself authorizes no batch, budget, traffic, pipeline treatment, or forecast credit.

Riley also rejected using unused paid-test capacity to increase Expansion Assist to four prompts per week. The proposal neither transferred unused authority nor changed the existing behavior-based eligibility, active-CS suppression, handoff rules, three-exposure ceiling, or causal, pipeline, revenue, and forecast boundaries. A one-page September operating-priorities brief preserved paid traffic off, Owen’s routine monthly source cycle, Growth’s reminder as nonproduction only, the separation between CS coordination design and later preflight, and Riley’s claim, correction, incident-stop, and disputed-semantics responsibilities.

Riley repeatedly corrected executive language. A favorable experiment completed its 21-day powered window with 8,302 assigned sessions: control 12.0%, treatment 12.6%, a favorable 0.6-point difference with a 95% CI of 0.1–1.1, below the predeclared 0.8-point minimum effect. The August 3–9 stabilization cohort showed control 12.1% versus treatment 12.5%, a 0.4-point difference with CI -0.3–1.1, weakening rather than strengthening the case. The run was closed without rollout. Riley created a training example emphasizing that a statistically favorable estimate can still fail the decision threshold.

Tomás later drafted that Helio Start “generated $27,860 in revenue and proved the paid motion can scale.” Riley rejected those additions and supplied the narrower audited statement: 25 workspaces admitted April 12–May 17, 18 paid-active, $27,860 in refund-adjusted collected cash, support effort of 33 minutes median and 116 minutes at the 90th percentile, five above 90 minutes, and no second Q3 batch authorized. Tomás retained ownership of the final board narrative, but no causal, scale, revenue, pipeline, or forecast claim was permitted.

Pricing-page assisted-route copy was also governed semantically. The rejected `Start setup` CTA was replaced by `Get setup help`, while the current CTA had been `Talk to an expert`; all pointed to the Customer Success assisted path. Riley assessed `Get setup help` as honest only if the destination and telemetry remained unchanged. Daniela released it after verifying the assisted path and existing event key; eligibility, admission, routing, telemetry, and authority were unchanged, and `Start setup` was not released. In another case, an entitlement source still showed `Team Annual` while the customer supplied confirmation that the correct label was `Business Annual` effective August 26. Because the template correctly rendered the governed source, Riley held the row, required source-owner correction, prohibited a template-only override, and allowed unaffected audiences to proceed only after their own complete preflight.

Riley’s personal health decisions retained the same conservative method. Earlier, a clinical check had cleared two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs weekly but not 40-minute runs or a third session; Riley completed symptom-free 30-minute runs and did not infer outdoor-bike clearance. On August 20 Riley requested a comparison of the posted summary with the prior day’s clinician decision, explicitly without treating the records check as new clearance. Riley then completed the first newly permitted 35-minute continuous easy run on August 22. There was no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or later symptom, and walking and stairs remained symptom-free the next morning. Riley kept the run off a commute day, did not add a third run or extra bike day, continued strengthening, and recognized that one result did not complete the required six-run tolerance period.

Riley and Sam’s Cherrywood renewal process moved from neutral comparison to acceptance. The proposed monthly total rose from $2,690 to $2,780, a $90 monthly/$1,080 annual increase. Cherrywood still supports both commutes, Riley’s workroom and painting corner, and Kibo’s quieter interior space. A nonbinding moving estimate was $2,080–$2,560 nonrefundable, comprising $1,780–$2,260 labor/vehicle, $180 packing materials, and $120 utility/account setup; refundable deposit and alternative-home rent remained excluded unknowns. After reviewing the confirmed early-vacate clarification, costs, preferences, and practical burden of moving, Riley and Sam accepted the December 1, 2027–November 30, 2028 renewal and planned to complete their own portal signatures before September 1 at 5:00pm Central. Riley requested an acceptance note that did not imply signing for Sam.

Kibo’s subscription vendor initially displayed a $66.50 one-time retail price instead of the retained $63.20 subscription price because of a catalog migration. The vendor corrected it to $63.20 with $0 shipping, preserving the 24-pound product, six-week frequency, and subscription status. Once processed, the order showed the corrected $63.20 merchandise price, no $66.50 charge, and unchanged terms; the discrepancy was resolved.

Family and household administration remained evidence-preserving. Mom’s 2028 Golden State Rx Saver notice listed a $38.20 monthly premium, $650 deductible, preferred in-network River Park Community Pharmacy, $0 copays for tier-1 lisinopril and atorvastatin, and Ventolin at $52 after the deductible. Verified 2027 terms were $35.40 monthly, a $615 deductible, the same $0 generic copays, and Ventolin at $49. Mom did not assume automatic renewal and chose to compare all options after competing materials arrive; an October 17, 2027, 11:00–11:30am Central review was scheduled, with Mom retaining the decision and no enrollment action taken.

Marcus reported that 18 seniors completed intake-week questionnaires but the week was crowded and some were already spiraling about deadlines. Riley sent encouragement and urged him to protect one ordinary evening from essay work. Marcus also found the retained March 14 scan-export manifest and checksum for family photograph P027. The cloud copy matched the preservation-master byte count and full SHA-256, while the local copy differed and remained nonauthoritative. The cloud copy was therefore identified as the preservation master; the local copy remained a working copy, and P027 stayed tied to an April 1994 Portland garden outing with the exact day unresolved.

Riley’s creative practice remained restrained and process-oriented. For a fully dry watercolor underpainting with a cool shadow beside a pale ceramic edge, Riley wanted one edge section to disappear and another remain crisp without lifting, scrubbing, or increasing orange saturation. The requested method was a small value test, controlled rewetting beside rather than over the pale edge, and full drying before judgment. In a separate interior study, two value thumbnails were compared: the centered window felt static, while the left-offset window with a larger quiet dark shape better supported a quiet rather than decorative emphasis. Riley also continued preserving disappearing edges, avoiding overworked blooms, testing minimal lifts, and maintaining the life of the paper.

Overall, Riley remains conscientious, vigilant, evidence-oriented, and protective of both customers and personal boundaries. Across experimentation, lifecycle operations, executive reporting, health, finances, relationships, household administration, family decisions, archives, and creative work, Riley’s recurring pattern is to preserve source evidence, make uncertainty visible, fail closed on stale or conflicting information, avoid conflating eligibility with capability, keep authority explicit, and make every conclusion proportional to the evidence actually available."},"systemMessage":"[honcho] session-start ← injected directives + summary"}

Session summary: From February 2023 through September 1, 2027, Riley’s decisions consistently emphasize methodological integrity, customer and personal protection, explicit uncertainty, preservation of source evidence, and narrow, reversible steps. Riley distinguishes observation from causality, defines denominators and eligibility precisely, treats stale or conflicting information as a reason to hold rather than guess, and separates evidence of safe operation from evidence sufficient for retirement, launch, staffing, CAC, revenue, forecasts, board claims, or strategic decisions. Riley is analytical, skeptical of small samples and narrative pressure, careful with customer-facing language, protective of operating boundaries, and increasingly willing to delegate execution while retaining governance, exception, correction, refusal, disputed-semantics, incident-stop, and final-claim authority.

Riley owns or strongly influences activation, retention, lifecycle, growth measurement, experimentation, customer communications, and operational guardrails at Helio, a roughly 140-person post-Series B company with approximately $48 million ARR. Earlier work included reproducing a mid-segment churn spike of about 5.1% against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Pricing-tier and historical-February comparisons were flat, while onboarding timing showed approximately 3.1% churn for users activated before day seven versus 7.8% for users still unactivated when the fixed day-seven email was sent. Riley treated this as a state-timing signal rather than causal proof. An onboarding-trigger experiment later showed a pooled +3.1-point week-one retention improvement, p=0.04, n=420, with directional stabilization-cohort support. Riley checked sample-ratio mismatch, source, geography, device, and guardrails and did not ship from the first significant result; after QA, the flow reached 100% for mid-segment and growth tiers, excluding starter. A later artifact was traced to a Customer Success auto-onboarding outage rather than the lifecycle flag.

A pricing-page experiment testing simplified layout, packaging, and value-per-seat framing showed treatment 1.8 points worse than control, p=0.03, but a concurrent signup-form layout change contaminated interpretation. Riley and Owen independently matched the result; Riley rolled it back despite pressure to extend it and documented exposure rules, event flow, cohort cuts, calculations, CSVs, and the confound. Pricing experiments were thereafter not to run alongside structural page or layout changes. A staging visual-regression runner later evaluated a retired flag once; Riley refused to call that production exposure or decommission the key before dependency review. Daniela removed the hard-coded staging reference, reran checks with zero evaluations, confirmed no production dependency, and then decommissioned the flag while preserving the historical record.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. Riley guarded against definition drift when an old notebook disagreed with the v3 dashboard and a warehouse transform incorrectly treated `template_imported` as first integration. Template imports were excluded from v3; a corrected discovery view could support exploration but not unlock an experiment or beta gate.

The sub-50-seat self-serve tier, Helio Start, was treated as an operating-model decision rather than merely pricing or packaging. Riley identified implications for entitlements, seat caps, billing, workspace limits, permissions, imports, migrations, onboarding, support volume, sales-assist rules, and human-help boundaries. Fit was defined by deployment shape and administrative complexity, not logo size: a 35-seat account requiring SCIM and legal redlines could be less self-serve-ready than a 90-seat account with a simple deployment. Pricing guardrails remained separate from eligibility and product constraints. In May 2025, the qualified decision was yes in principle, but not as a quick toggle or public launch; foundations were estimated at roughly 12 weeks. Green cases generally had fewer than 50 seats, one workspace, a standard integration, one identifiable administrator, and no migration request. Yellow cases included multiple administrators, imports, unclear ownership, or difficult integrations. Red or assisted cases included SSO, complex permissions, high-volume migration, no clear owner, or custom onboarding. Riley rejected Q3/August launch language, kept discovery candidates separate from a beta pool, and required lifecycle language to route heavier-support accounts to assisted paths rather than imply they had failed a judgmental screen.

Expansion Assist targeted retained mid-segment v2 accounts with 75–200 seats. The nudge generated only about $4–$5 expansion MRR per account against an $8 target, with too small a sample for strategic claims. Signals concentrated among accounts with deeper integration use and multiple active administrators. In a 312-account table, 118 had at least three integrations, 141 had at least two active administrators, 39 had repeated plan-limit modals, and 37 had blocked ceiling actions. Expansion Assist remained separate from Helio Start, churn, pipeline credit, forecasts, and Q3 revenue claims. Its ceiling remained no more than three neutral, state-specific exposures per week, with active Customer Success work suppressing prompts and handoff rules preserved.

Ownership was deliberately divided: Owen handled routine source completeness and measurement; Ines handled lifecycle governance, copy boundaries, and message-state controls; Daniela handled source reliability, engineering release controls, and rollback; Customer Success handled staffed assistance; Marcus Vail controlled narrative treatment; Riley retained guardrails, exception decisions, customer corrections, incident stops, disputed semantics, executive tradeoffs, and final operating claims. Riley’s delegation produced relief but initially raised concern about not reclaiming work. Owen’s formal H2 mature-outcome-packet goal was later marked met because he used the correct denominator and dates, waited for all predeclared windows, led with owner certifications and measurement limits, and found no semantic dispute. This did not transfer board-readiness, causal, revenue, forecast, or executive-language authority; any future semantic dispute requires him to leave the review incomplete and escalate it. Ines’s connector-specific instructional-wording goal was also marked met after she independently carried a revision through review, supplied paired cases, preserved governed meanings, and left connector detection and release verification with Daniela. Her release ceiling and other authority limits remained unchanged.

The shared-state Customer Success auto-nudge system initially had four production consumers. Riley rejected Growth’s proposal to add a renewal-risk notification as a fifth because semantic mapping, field mapping, source-owner review, freshness limits, operator views, and rollback rehearsal were incomplete. The production feed remained at four consumers. The denominator rule remained one primary ledger row per scheduled nudge decision, with checks, holds, evaluation timestamps, and final disposition preserved in audit history; rechecks and holds did not create duplicate denominator rows.

A May 20 refresh caused 12 pending decisions to cross the freshness limit. The system held all 12 rather than reusing stale “no work” values. After the source was restored, fresh checks found eight with current active adoption or renewal work, becoming valid suppressions, and four with current no-work state, proceeding. No stale-state nudge was sent, no customer correction was needed, and rollback was unnecessary. Checkpoints recorded 327 unique scheduled decisions through May 22, 641 through May 29, and 846 through June 5, including 19, 31, and 39 fail-closed stale/conflicting decisions respectively. There were no differences across external-system authority, connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin, or Customer Success views. Riley treated this as interim evidence, not mature reliability or justification for retiring the legacy path.

In August, Growth’s first historical replay incorrectly omitted active-Customer-Success-work suppression because it argued that an in-product reminder was not a “send.” Riley ruled this a disputed interpretation, kept the replay incomplete, prohibited shadow and production work, and required Growth to implement suppression and rerun it. The corrected 240-record replay found 12 active/current CS-work records suppressed, nine missing or stale required states held fail-closed, and 219 current eligible records; there were no semantic disagreements, cross-surface mismatches, or customer-facing actions. Riley permitted only bounded nonproduction shadow work. The first shadow interval evaluated 96 live decisions: eight suppressed for active CS work, four held for stale state, and 84 reminder-eligible, with zero customer-facing reminders and no semantic or cross-surface disagreement. Riley declined production, requiring a complete shadow review, Riley’s customer-action approval, and Daniela’s release and rollback approval. The production count stayed at four.

The August Customer.io forecast estimated 1,620,000 baseline messages, 240,000 routine-campaign messages, and 110,000 transactional messages against a 2,000,000-message monthly allowance. Riley verified the 1.97 million total and 30,000-message headroom but kept that commercial capacity separate from Ines’s three-send weekly ceiling and all preflight and audit rules. The quarterly access review retained only existing scopes: Ines for lifecycle preflight and bounded routine-send release, Daniela’s engineering group for integration release and rollback, and Riley for customer correction and incident-stop decisions. The review added no authority.

The Helio Start paid-test decision was finalized in August. The fixed cohort contained 25 workspaces admitted April 12–May 17. Eighteen became paid-active, refund-adjusted collected cash was $27,860, and certified support effort was 33 minutes at the median and 116 minutes at the 90th percentile; five of 25 exceeded 90 support minutes, and four of those required coordination with a separate owner-level permission or network-allowlist holder. Priya and Riley did not authorize a second Q3 batch. Paid traffic remained off through September 30, with no additional budget, pipeline or forecast credit, and no implication of causal acquisition, revenue, support improvement, scale readiness, or forecast impact. The $360 remaining from the prior $8,000 cap was explicitly not continuing authorization and could not reopen traffic. Any later proposal requires Customer Success to define staffed ownership and service hours for the coordination, plus a fresh 24-case nonproduction preflight by Daniela and Ines showing preserved paid-source final-route attribution, governed-state meanings, lifecycle holds, and suppression behavior. Account-level support minutes must continue from first contact without resetting the clock.

Customer Success’s coordination-design brief initially lacked a capacity assumption. The completed design names the Customer Success setup desk as primary owner, with the on-duty Customer Success manager as backup, during 8:00am–6:00pm Central Monday through Friday. It can support a future capped run of no more than 25 admitted workspaces without displacing ordinary assisted coverage. The handoff trigger is an admitted workspace requiring owner-level permission or network-allowlist action; transferred context includes connector, external-authority state, required owner action, admitting route, first-contact time, and support notes. Initial response is within two business hours, after-hours cases queue until opening, and the CS lead escalates if no owner accepts. Riley accepted the staffing section as complete but kept the 24-case preflight and any paid batch pending. The design itself authorizes no batch, budget, traffic, pipeline treatment, or forecast credit.

Riley also rejected using unused paid-test capacity to increase Expansion Assist to four prompts per week. The proposal neither transferred unused authority nor changed the existing behavior-based eligibility, active-CS suppression, handoff rules, three-exposure ceiling, or causal, pipeline, revenue, and forecast boundaries. A one-page September operating-priorities brief preserved paid traffic off, Owen’s routine monthly source cycle, Growth’s reminder as nonproduction only, the separation between CS coordination design and later preflight, and Riley’s claim, correction, incident-stop, and disputed-semantics responsibilities.

Riley repeatedly corrected executive language. A favorable experiment completed its 21-day powered window with 8,302 assigned sessions: control 12.0%, treatment 12.6%, a favorable 0.6-point difference with a 95% CI of 0.1–1.1, below the predeclared 0.8-point minimum effect. The August 3–9 stabilization cohort showed control 12.1% versus treatment 12.5%, a 0.4-point difference with CI -0.3–1.1, weakening rather than strengthening the case. The run was closed without rollout. Riley created a training example emphasizing that a statistically favorable estimate can still fail the decision threshold.

Tomás later drafted that Helio Start “generated $27,860 in revenue and proved the paid motion can scale.” Riley rejected those additions and supplied the narrower audited statement: 25 workspaces admitted April 12–May 17, 18 paid-active, $27,860 in refund-adjusted collected cash, support effort of 33 minutes median and 116 minutes at the 90th percentile, five above 90 minutes, and no second Q3 batch authorized. Tomás retained ownership of the final board narrative, but no causal, scale, revenue, pipeline, or forecast claim was permitted.

Pricing-page assisted-route copy was also governed semantically. The rejected `Start setup` CTA was replaced by `Get setup help`, while the current CTA had been `Talk to an expert`; all pointed to the Customer Success assisted path. Riley assessed `Get setup help` as honest only if the destination and telemetry remained unchanged. Daniela released it after verifying the assisted path and existing event key; eligibility, admission, routing, telemetry, and authority were unchanged, and `Start setup` was not released. In another case, an entitlement source still showed `Team Annual` while the customer supplied confirmation that the correct label was `Business Annual` effective August 26. Because the template correctly rendered the governed source, Riley held the row, required source-owner correction, prohibited a template-only override, and allowed unaffected audiences to proceed only after their own complete preflight.

Riley’s personal health decisions retained the same conservative method. Earlier, a clinical check had cleared two nonconsecutive 30-minute continuous easy runs weekly but not 40-minute runs or a third session; Riley completed symptom-free 30-minute runs and did not infer outdoor-bike clearance. On August 20 Riley requested a comparison of the posted summary with the prior day’s clinician decision, explicitly without treating the records check as new clearance. Riley then completed the first newly permitted 35-minute continuous easy run on August 22. There was no focal ankle pain, swelling, instability, gait change, or later symptom, and walking and stairs remained symptom-free the next morning. Riley kept the run off a commute day, did not add a third run or extra bike day, continued strengthening, and recognized that one result did not complete the required six-run tolerance period.

Cherrywood still supports both commutes, Riley’s workroom and painting corner, and Kibo’s quieter interior space. A nonbinding moving estimate was $2,080–$2,560 nonrefundable, comprising $1,780–$2,260 labor/vehicle, $180 packing materials, and $120 utility/account setup; refundable deposit and alternative-home rent remained excluded unknowns. After reviewing the confirmed early-vacate clarification, costs, preferences, and practical burden of moving, Riley and Sam accepted the December 1, 2027–November 30, 2028 renewal and planned to complete their own portal signatures before September 1 at 5:00pm Central. input.body:
## Standing practice

The investigation-readout framework (hypothesis stack + effect size + stabilization cohort) is the **default readout practice for Growth and Customer Success**, effective since Q1 2024. It is not a companywide mandate.

## Who it applies to

- Growth-team experiment summaries
- Customer Success renewal-risk / churn readouts

Ownership stays team-distributed, not centralized:
- **Owen** owns standard readout shape — denominator, effect size, conclusion order.
- **Ines** owns lifecycle-risk / audience-risk language.

## Non-negotiables (do not flex, even in lightweight use)

1. **Effect size travels with the conclusion** — observed effect and decision-relevant (minimum-to-change-the-call) effect are stated before any recommendation, not just the hypothesis-stack shape.
2. **First significance ≠ ship** — once a result crosses significance, hold for one additional stabilization cohort before rollout. A first-significant result is reported as "promising, pending stabilization," not as final.

## Limits on template and approval requirements

- This is **guidance, not a required companywide template**. Teams outside Growth/CS are not obligated to adopt it.
- There is **no approval queue** — readouts do not need to route through Riley, Owen, or Ines for sign-off before teams act on them. Owen and Ines are named reviewers for their respective lanes, available on request, not gatekeepers.
- The practice is meant to be self-sustaining: a 2024-03 audit of twelve Growth/CS readouts confirmed teams were applying the checklist and the two non-negotiables correctly without routing decisions back through a central approver.

Session summary: From February 2023 through September 1, 2027, Riley’s decisions consistently emphasize methodological integrity, customer and personal protection, explicit uncertainty, preservation of source evidence, and narrow, reversible steps. Riley distinguishes observation from causality, defines denominators and eligibility precisely, treats stale or conflicting information as a reason to hold rather than guess, and separates evidence of safe operation from evidence sufficient for retirement, launch, staffing, CAC, revenue, forecasts, board claims, or strategic decisions. Riley is analytical, skeptical of small samples and narrative pressure, careful with customer-facing language, protective of operating boundaries, and increasingly willing to delegate execution while retaining governance, exception, correction, refusal, disputed-semantics, incident-stop, and final-claim authority.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. ## Helio Start Change-Sequencing Checklist (as of 2026-09-21)

### 1. Packaging changes
**Must be settled first:**
- Event taxonomy + entitlement instrumentation (admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, entitlement state) — the standing engineering-scoping gate from the Jun 22 leadership readout.
- No `plan_name → entitlement` inference — packaging tiers must resolve entitlement from actual entitlement state, not plan name.
- Naming must stay in discovery_/fit_/assisted vocabulary — no launch/beta/refusal framing baked into tier or feature names.

**Blocks downstream:**
- Any pricing-page experiment (packaging is the input to what the test displays/sells).
- Paid acquisition (ad-facing packaging claims depend on stable entitlement-backed tiers).

---

### 2. Pricing-page experiment
**Must be settled first:**
- Packaging/entitlement instrumentation complete (item 1).
- Activation definition frozen (currently v3) — the metric the experiment will read out on can't be redefined mid-test.
- No concurrent page/layout changes during the test window — copy/content edits are fine, structural changes are not.

**Blocks downstream:**
- Any GA/launch decision — requires a full 21-day powered read (effect + CI); interim reads are guardrails-only, not stop/ship signals.
- Any ship decision also requires a stabilization cohort after first significance — first significance ≠ ship.
- Paid acquisition should not be scoped or budgeted off an unstabilized or interim pricing-page read.

---

### 3. Paid acquisition
**Must be settled first:**
- Stabilized pricing-page/packaging result (item 2 fully closed, not interim).
- Separate, explicit budget authorization for this specific batch — prior approvals don't carry forward to a new batch, spend cap, or channel.
- Connector/outreach permission checked independently — applicant or lead quality never substitutes for the outreach-permission step (external authority ≠ outreach permission).
- Eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and assisted-routing rules reconfirmed unchanged for this batch.

**Blocks downstream:**
- Activation/support-load measurement attributed to paid cohorts (can't measure a channel that isn't authorized/instrumented).
- Any forecast, pipeline, or revenue claim — paid-acquisition approval itself never grants forecast credit or a second-batch authorization; each must be requested separately.

---

### 4. Activation measurement
**Must be settled first:**
- Activation definition version frozen for the measurement window (don't change v1/v2/v3 mid-read).
- Held-not-queued semantics applied — held/pending admission records get fresh per-record eval before being counted in any denominator, not auto-included once data catches up.
- Assisted-CTA counted as a separate measure — never relabeled as eligibility-flow starts, admissions, pipeline, or forecast evidence.

**Blocks downstream:**
- Any board/executive claim drawing on Helio Start activation numbers.
- Any cross-lane comparison or aggregate reporting.

---

### Required separation between measurement populations
- **Helio Start vs. mid-segment/Expansion Assist**: Helio Start metrics must stay in their own reporting layer, never merged into retained mid-segment or Expansion Assist numbers.
- **Assisted-CTA vs. eligibility-flow**: assisted-CTA activity is a distinct measure, not folded into eligibility-flow starts/admissions/pipeline/forecast.
- **Pricing-page test population vs. concurrent changes**: no other structural page change may run against the same population during an active pricing-page test.
- **Held/pending records vs. counted records**: held admissions stay out of denominators until individually re-evaluated — never auto-promoted into the active measurement population.

---

**Net sequencing:** Packaging (entitlement gate) → Pricing-page experiment (frozen activation def, no concurrent changes, full powered read + stabilization cohort) → Paid acquisition (fresh budget approval + outreach-permission check) → Activation measurement (versioned definition, held-not-queued, assisted-CTA kept separate) → any board/forecast claim.

Session summary: From February 2023 through September 1, 2027, Riley’s decisions consistently emphasize methodological integrity, customer and personal protection, explicit uncertainty, preservation of source evidence, and narrow, reversible steps. Riley distinguishes observation from causality, defines denominators and eligibility precisely, treats stale or conflicting information as a reason to hold rather than guess, and separates evidence of safe operation from evidence sufficient for retirement, launch, staffing, CAC, revenue, forecasts, board claims, or strategic decisions. Riley is analytical, skeptical of small samples and narrative pressure, careful with customer-facing language, protective of operating boundaries, and increasingly willing to delegate execution while retaining governance, exception, correction, refusal, disputed-semantics, incident-stop, and final-claim authority.

Riley owns or strongly influences activation, retention, lifecycle, growth measurement, experimentation, customer communications, and operational guardrails at Helio, a roughly 140-person post-Series B company with approximately $48 million ARR. Earlier work included reproducing a mid-segment churn spike of about 5.1% against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Pricing-tier and historical-February comparisons were flat, while onboarding timing showed approximately 3.1% churn for users activated before day seven versus 7.8% for users still unactivated when the fixed day-seven email was sent. Riley treated this as a state-timing signal rather than causal proof. An onboarding-trigger experiment later showed a pooled +3.1-point week-one retention improvement, p=0.04, n=420, with directional stabilization-cohort support. Riley checked sample-ratio mismatch, source, geography, device, and guardrails and did not ship from the first significant result; after QA, the flow reached 100% for mid-segment and growth tiers, excluding starter. A later artifact was traced to a Customer Success auto-onboarding outage rather than the lifecycle flag.

A pricing-page experiment testing simplified layout, packaging, and value-per-seat framing showed treatment 1.8 points worse than control, p=0.03, but a concurrent signup-form layout change contaminated interpretation. Riley and Owen independently matched the result; Riley rolled it back despite pressure to extend it and documented exposure rules, event flow, cohort cuts, calculations, CSVs, and the confound. Pricing experiments were thereafter not to run alongside structural page or layout changes. A staging visual-regression runner later evaluated a retired flag once; Riley refused to call that production exposure or decommission the key before dependency review. Daniela removed the hard-coded staging reference, reran checks with zero evaluations, confirmed no production dependency, and then decommissioned the flag while preserving the historical record.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. Riley guarded against definition drift when an old notebook disagreed with the v3 dashboard and a warehouse transform incorrectly treated `template_imported` as first integration. Template imports were excluded from v3; a corrected discovery view could support exploration but not unlock an experiment or beta gate.

The sub-50-seat self-serve tier, Helio Start, was treated as an operating-model decision rather than merely pricing or packaging. Riley identified implications for entitlements, seat caps, billing, workspace limits, permissions, imports, migrations, onboarding, support volume, sales-assist rules, and human-help boundaries. Fit was defined by deployment shape and administrative complexity, not logo size: a 35-seat account requiring SCIM and legal redlines could be less self-serve-ready than a 90-seat account with a simple deployment. Pricing guardrails remained separate from eligibility and product constraints. In May 2025, the qualified decision was yes in principle, but not as a quick toggle or public launch; foundations were estimated at roughly 12 weeks. Green cases generally had fewer than 50 seats, one workspace, a standard integration, one identifiable administrator, and no migration request. Yellow cases included multiple administrators, imports, unclear ownership, or difficult integrations. Red or assisted cases included SSO, complex permissions, high-volume migration, no clear owner, or custom onboarding. Riley rejected Q3/August launch language, kept discovery candidates separate from a beta pool, and required lifecycle language to route heavier-support accounts to assisted paths rather than imply they had failed a judgmental screen.

Expansion Assist targeted retained mid-segment v2 accounts with 75–200 seats. The nudge generated only about $4–$5 expansion MRR per account against an $8 target, with too small a sample for strategic claims. Signals concentrated among accounts with deeper integration use and multiple active administrators. In a 312-account table, 118 had at least three integrations, 141 had at least two active administrators, 39 had repeated plan-limit modals, and 37 had blocked ceiling actions. Expansion Assist remained separate from Helio Start, churn, pipeline credit, forecasts, and Q3 revenue claims. Its ceiling remained no more than three neutral, state-specific exposures per week, with active Customer Success work suppressing prompts and handoff rules preserved.

Ownership was deliberately divided: Owen handled routine source completeness and measurement; Ines handled lifecycle governance, copy boundaries, and message-state controls; Daniela handled source reliability, engineering release controls, and rollback; Customer Success handled staffed assistance; Marcus Vail controlled narrative treatment; Riley retained guardrails, exception decisions, customer corrections, incident stops, disputed semantics, executive tradeoffs, and final operating claims. Low-depth slice: 0-1 integration or only 1 active admin in the last 14 days; n=142; treatment +$0.60 expansion MRR/account versus control
Middle-depth remainder: directionally positive but below the bar
Owen note: "This looks behavior-gated, not day-60 gated. I would not widen the current flag without a new eligibility model."

[2024-11-25T11:30:00-06:00] A different account exposed on October 14 expanded from 80 to 100 seats after a Customer Success options review. Owen can record this as the second observed within-window expansion in the second cohort, but the cohort has no randomized control and the outcome is not attributed to the prompt. This does not reopen exposure, alter eligibility, or become pipeline or forecast evidence. The remaining outcome windows continue to mature.

Post the 80-to-100-seat expansion to growth operations with those noncausal, nonpipeline, nonforecast, and closed-exposure boundaries.

[2023-05-21T16:00:00-05:00] ok so i finally pinned the expansion thing enough to write it down. EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge. keeping it tight: retained mid-seg only, 75-200 seats, v2 accounts, hit them with the in-product prompt at day 60 and see if we can get at least +$8 expansion MRR per acct. flag is `expansion_nudge_60d_v1`. starting at 25% -- don't want a giant splash before we know the copy/placement isn't junk -- and the window is 2 weeks if the power math holds. in parallel with the sub-50-seat doc still, which is annoying but also kind of the same pattern as before. two tracks, one more strategic, one just ship the test.

[2023-06-22T13:05:00-05:00] I reviewed the expansion-nudge prompt copy and placement with Ines after Owen's depth split. The prompt is in the usage panel after day 60, and the copy is direct but not obviously wrong for the low-depth slice, so we didn't find a copy or placement issue big enough to explain why low-depth accounts are nearly flat. Marcus then asked whether we should widen `expansion_nudge_60d_v1` for the high-depth slice, and my answer is no: that would change eligibility after launch, overfit the slice, and turn a partial read into a fake broad answer. Please update the experiment record for EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge to status "inconclusive" with the result that the aggregate remained below the +$8 bar while high-depth active-admin accounts were materially ahead and low-depth accounts were nearly flat. Add the learning carryforward that the follow-on path should use behavior-based eligibility rather than a blanket day-60 prompt. Also add a note to the `expansion_nudge_60d_v1` feature flag that rollout stays at 25% and eligibility should not be widened from this read.

[2024-09-30T11:40:00-05:00] Priya and I made the quarter-end Expansion Assist decision after reviewing the completed pilot. The timing concentration was meaningful for designing the next cohort: all six expansions and seven of eight help requests came from the 12 exposed accounts whose product-visible usage ceiling had been crossed within the preceding 14 days. That remains descriptive evidence without a control, so we declined a broad rollout and approved a second bounded Q4 cohort instead. Eligibility still requires deeper integration use and recent behavior by a qualifying human admin who remains active when eligibility is checked, and active Customer Success adoption or renewal work suppresses the commercial prompt. For this cohort, the product-visible usage ceiling must have been newly crossed within the preceding 14 days. The cohort is capped at 18 accounts with no more than three exposures per week, using neutral help-or-options treatment and state-specific messaging. The old day-60 basis is retired, Expansion Assist remains outside pipeline and forecast reporting, and there was no second-cohort exposure on September 30.

[2023-06-08T09:27:00-05:00] Owen's next cut on EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge is finally more informative than the n=92 snapshot, but I'm still trying to keep everyone from getting ahead of the data. Treatment is still ahead, around +$5 expansion MRR per account versus control, but the sample is still modest and it's below the original +$8 bar. The lift also isn't broad — it's mostly in accounts with deeper integration usage and more than one active admin. Marcus is already tempted to call it a retained-mid expansion win. I want a measured readout I can use with Marcus, Owen, and Ines: the experiment stays narrow, no copy change, the next cut needs to split integration depth and active-admin count explicitly, and the working hypothesis is usage-readiness rather than a generic day-60 prompt win. Can you draft that?

[2023-06-29T12:32:00-05:00] We just met on the expansion-nudge read, and I want the experiment record updated so nobody later reads June as a hidden ship decision. Please update EXP-2023-05-expansion-nudge to status "inconclusive" with landed_at 2023-06-29. The result should say the aggregate lift settled below the +$8 expansion MRR per-account bar and the experiment should not become a blanket rollout. Session summary: From February 2023 through September 1, 2027, Riley’s decisions consistently emphasize methodological integrity, customer and personal protection, explicit uncertainty, preservation of source evidence, and narrow, reversible steps. Riley distinguishes observation from causality, defines denominators and eligibility precisely, treats stale or conflicting information as a reason to hold rather than guess, and separates evidence of safe operation from evidence sufficient for retirement, launch, staffing, CAC, revenue, forecasts, board claims, or strategic decisions. Riley is analytical, skeptical of small samples and narrative pressure, careful with customer-facing language, protective of operating boundaries, and increasingly willing to delegate execution while retaining governance, exception, correction, refusal, disputed-semantics, incident-stop, and final-claim authority.

Riley owns or strongly influences activation, retention, lifecycle, growth measurement, experimentation, customer communications, and operational guardrails at Helio, a roughly 140-person post-Series B company with approximately $48 million ARR. Earlier work included reproducing a mid-segment churn spike of about 5.1% against a 2.1% trailing-six-month baseline. Pricing-tier and historical-February comparisons were flat, while onboarding timing showed approximately 3.1% churn for users activated before day seven versus 7.8% for users still unactivated when the fixed day-seven email was sent. Riley treated this as a state-timing signal rather than causal proof. An onboarding-trigger experiment later showed a pooled +3.1-point week-one retention improvement, p=0.04, n=420, with directional stabilization-cohort support. Riley checked sample-ratio mismatch, source, geography, device, and guardrails and did not ship from the first significant result; after QA, the flow reached 100% for mid-segment and growth tiers, excluding starter. A later artifact was traced to a Customer Success auto-onboarding outage rather than the lifecycle flag.

A pricing-page experiment testing simplified layout, packaging, and value-per-seat framing showed treatment 1.8 points worse than control, p=0.03, but a concurrent signup-form layout change contaminated interpretation. Riley and Owen independently matched the result; Riley rolled it back despite pressure to extend it and documented exposure rules, event flow, cohort cuts, calculations, CSVs, and the confound. Pricing experiments were thereafter not to run alongside structural page or layout changes. A staging visual-regression runner later evaluated a retired flag once; Riley refused to call that production exposure or decommission the key before dependency review. Daniela removed the hard-coded staging reference, reran checks with zero evaluations, confirmed no production dependency, and then decommissioned the flag while preserving the historical record.

Activation measurement was revised because v2—first integration plus two logins within 14 days—was too UI-shaped and could exclude successful integrations with flowing data. Version 3 became first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v1 and v2 tables were retained. Riley guarded against definition drift when an old notebook disagreed with the v3 dashboard and a warehouse transform incorrectly treated `template_imported` as first integration. Template imports were excluded from v3; a corrected discovery view could support exploration but not unlock an experiment or beta gate.

The sub-50-seat self-serve tier, Helio Start, was treated as an operating-model decision rather than merely pricing or packaging. Riley identified implications for entitlements, seat caps, billing, workspace limits, permissions, imports, migrations, onboarding, support volume, sales-assist rules, and human-help boundaries. Fit was defined by deployment shape and administrative complexity, not logo size: a 35-seat account requiring SCIM and legal redlines could be less self-serve-ready than a 90-seat account with a simple deployment. Pricing guardrails remained separate from eligibility and product constraints. In May 2025, the qualified decision was yes in principle, but not as a quick toggle or public launch; foundations were estimated at roughly 12 weeks. Green cases generally had fewer than 50 seats, one workspace, a standard integration, one identifiable administrator, and no migration request. Yellow cases included multiple administrators, imports, unclear ownership, or difficult integrations. Red or assisted cases included SSO, complex permissions, high-volume migration, no clear owner, or custom onboarding. Riley rejected Q3/August launch language, kept discovery candidates separate from a beta pool, and required lifecycle language to route heavier-support accounts to assisted paths rather than imply they had failed a judgmental screen.

Expansion Assist targeted retained mid-segment v2 accounts with 75–200 seats. The nudge generated only about $4–$5 expansion MRR per account against an $8 target, with too small a sample for strategic claims. Signals concentrated among accounts with deeper integration use and multiple active administrators. In a 312-account table, 118 had at least three integrations, 141 had at least two active administrators, 39 had repeated plan-limit modals, and 37 had blocked ceiling actions. Expansion Assist remained separate from Helio Start, churn, pipeline credit, forecasts, and Q3 revenue claims. Its ceiling remained no more than three neutral, state-specific exposures per week, with active Customer Success work suppressing prompts and handoff rules preserved.

Ownership was deliberately divided: Owen handled routine source completeness and measurement; Ines handled lifecycle governance, copy boundaries, and message-state controls; Daniela handled source reliability, engineering release controls, and rollback; Customer Success handled staffed assistance; Marcus Vail controlled narrative treatment; Riley retained guardrails, exception decisions, customer corrections, incident stops, disputed semantics, executive tradeoffs, and final operating claims. Riley’s delegation produced relief but initially raised concern about not reclaiming work. Owen’s formal H2 mature-outcome-packet goal was later marked met because he used the correct denominator and dates, waited for all predeclared windows, led with owner certifications and measurement limits, and found no semantic dispute. This did not transfer board-readiness, causal, revenue, forecast, or executive-language authority; any future semantic dispute requires him to leave the review incomplete and escalate it. Ines’s connector-specific instructional-wording goal was also marked met after she independently carried a revision through review, supplied paired cases, preserved governed meanings, and left connector detection and release verification with Daniela. Her release ceiling and other authority limits remained unchanged.

The shared-state Customer Success auto-nudge system initially had four production consumers. Riley rejected Growth’s proposal to add a renewal-risk notification as a fifth because semantic mapping, field mapping, source-owner review, freshness limits, operator views, and rollback rehearsal were incomplete. The production feed remained at four consumers. The denominator rule remained one primary ledger row per scheduled nudge decision, with checks, holds, evaluation timestamps, and final disposition preserved in audit history; rechecks and holds did not create duplicate denominator rows.

A May 20 refresh caused 12 pending decisions to cross the freshness limit. The system held all 12 rather than reusing stale “no work” values. After the source was restored, fresh checks found eight with current active adoption or renewal work, becoming valid suppressions, and four with current no-work state, proceeding. No stale-state nudge was sent, no customer correction was needed, and rollback was unnecessary. Checkpoints recorded 327 unique scheduled decisions through May 22, 641 through May 29, and 846 through June 5, including 19, 31, and 39 fail-closed stale/conflicting decisions respectively. There were no differences across external-system authority, connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin, or Customer Success views. Riley treated this as interim evidence, not mature reliability or justification for retiring the legacy path.

In August, Growth’s first historical replay incorrectly omitted active-Customer-Success-work suppression because it argued that an in-product reminder was not a “send.” Riley ruled this a disputed interpretation, kept the replay incomplete, prohibited shadow and production work, and required Growth to implement suppression and rerun it. The August Customer.io forecast estimated 1,620,000 baseline messages, 240,000 routine-campaign messages, and 110,000 transactional messages against a 2,000,000-message monthly allowance. Riley verified the 1.97 million total and 30,000-message headroom but kept that commercial capacity separate from Ines’s three-send weekly ceiling and all preflight and audit rules. The quarterly access review retained only existing scopes: Ines for lifecycle preflight and bounded routine-send release, Daniela’s engineering group for integration release and rollback, and Riley for customer correction and incident-stop decisions. The review added no authority.

Eighteen became paid-active, refund-adjusted collected cash was $27,860, and certified support effort was 33 minutes at the median and 116 minutes at the 90th percentile; five of 25 exceeded 90 support minutes, and four of those required coordination with a separate owner-level permission or network-allowlist holder. Priya and Riley did not authorize a second Q3 batch. Paid traffic remained off through September 30, with no additional budget, pipeline or forecast credit, and no implication of causal acquisition, revenue, support improvement, scale readiness, or forecast impact. The $360 remaining from the prior $8,000 cap was explicitly not continuing authorization and could not reopen traffic. Any later proposal requires Customer Success to define staffed ownership and service hours for the coordination, plus a fresh 24-case nonproduction preflight by Daniela and Ines showing preserved paid-source final-route attribution, governed-state meanings, lifecycle holds, and suppression behavior. Account-level support minutes must continue from first contact without resetting the clock.
